planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained potting mix or garden soil in bright to deep shade with high humidity; this miniature selection suits terrariums, dish gardens, and shaded container plantings as readily as ground beds in frost-free climates.

directions: A miniature, tightly tufted form of delta maidenhair distinguished by very small, closely set leaflets on fine black stems, giving a denser and more compact silhouette than the species at roughly half its size. It needs the same consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained mix and high humidity as other tropical maidenhairs and will brown quickly in dry air, direct sun, or cold drafts. Outdoors it survives only in sheltered, humid zone 10-12 sites; elsewhere grow it as a choice small houseplant, terrarium subject, or shaded patio container specimen. Mist regularly and divide crowded crowns in spring as the pot fills.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in consistently moist, gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright to dappled shade in spring; this dwarf coastal selection suits rock gardens, troughs, and container culture where its diminutive scale can be appreciated up close.

directions: A naturally dwarf selection of western maidenhair, originally collected from the Haida Gwaii archipelago, that stays under 8 inches tall with densely tufted, fan-shaped blue-green fronds on glossy black-purple stems — a fraction of the size of the straight species. It suits shaded rock gardens, alpine troughs, and container plantings where its fine texture and compact habit read as a jewel-like accent rather than the larger drifts formed by typical western maidenhair. Keep soil evenly moist and sheltered from drying wind, mulching lightly with leaf litter over winter in the colder part of its range. Divide congested crowns in early spring, keeping divisions from drying out before replanting.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in bright to full shade in spring, barely covering the shallow rhizome; keep soil consistently moist while the clump establishes.

directions: A rare English selection of the native northern maidenhair distinguished by soft chartreuse-gold new foliage that holds its color better than most yellow-leaved ferns before mellowing slightly with age, carried on the same wiry, glossy black stems and horseshoe-shaped, fan-divided fronds as the species. Site it in bright to full shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil, since both harsh sun and drought will scorch the pale foliage quickly. It combines beautifully with dark-leaved hostas, hellebores, or Solomon's seal, where the golden color reads as a highlight against deeper greens. Divide congested clumps in early spring, keeping divisions moist until replanted; deer generally leave it alone.

planting.note: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade near a pond edge or boggy border, the same culture as the straight species.

directions: A textural selection of royal fern in which the margins of the pinnules are crisped and undulating rather than flat, giving the coarsely divided, locust-like foliage a rippled, ruffled appearance distinct from the forked tufts of the crested 'Cristata' form. Culture is identical to plain royal fern: provide constantly moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil at a pond margin, stream bank, or rain garden in partial shade, where it tolerates standing water better than almost any other hardy fern. It is somewhat less vigorous and slightly shorter than the straight species, so plant it where the rippled frond texture can be seen at close range. Foliage turns golden-bronze in fall before dying back for winter; divide congested clumps in spring if needed.
